title: Pandas (Data Analysis & Manipulation)
description: Series, DataFrames, data cleaning, GroupBy aggregations, merging/joining, MultiIndex analysis, vectorized string operations, and DateTime.

lessons.title: 1D Series Object & Statistical Aggregations
lessons.concept_markdown:
A Pandas `Series` is a one-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data type. Unlike NumPy arrays, Series support axis labels (index):
- `pd.Series(data, index=...)`: Creates a Series
- Summary statistics: `.sum()`, `.mean()`, `.median()`, `.std()`, `.min()`, `.max()`
- `.value_counts()`: Returns frequency of unique values in descending order

code_walkthroughs.title: Series Statistical Summaries
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print('Mean:', s.mean(), 'Max:', s.max())
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Calculates arithmetic mean and maximum value directly across the Series.

practice_challenges.title: Filter Series Above Mean
practice_challenges.description: Read a space-separated line of numbers from input. Create a Pandas Series. Calculate its mean. Print how many values in the Series are strictly greater than the mean.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# Read numbers, create Series, count elements > mean
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([float(x) for x in input().split()])
mean_val = s.mean()
count_above = (s > mean_val).sum()
print(int(count_above))

hints.level_1_nudge: Compute mean using s.mean(), then evaluate (s > mean_val).sum().
hints.level_2_strategy: The boolean mask (s > mean_val) converts True to 1 and False to 0 when summed.

lessons.title: 2D Tabular Data & loc vs iloc
lessons.concept_markdown:
A `DataFrame` is a two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different types:
- `df['col']`: Selects a column as a Series
- `df[['col1', 'col2']]`: Selects multiple columns as a sub-DataFrame
- `df.iloc[row_idx, col_idx]`: Integer position-based indexing
- `df.loc[row_label, col_label]`: Label-based indexing

code_walkthroughs.title: Creating and Filtering DataFrame
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'], 'Age': [25, 30, 22]})
print(df[df['Age'] >= 25]['Name'].tolist())
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Filters rows where `Age >= 25` and extracts the `'Name'` column as a list.

practice_challenges.title: Filter High Earners
practice_challenges.description: Read an integer `N` (number of rows). Then read `N` lines formatted as `'Name Salary'` (e.g. `'Alice 75000'`). Create a DataFrame with columns `['Name', 'Salary']`. Filter rows where `Salary >= 50000`, sorted by `Salary` in descending order. Print the names space-separated.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
# Create DataFrame and filter salaries >= 50000
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
data = []
for _ in range(n):
    parts = input().split()
    data.append({'Name': parts[0], 'Salary': float(parts[1])})
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
high_earners = df[df['Salary'] >= 50000].sort_values(by='Salary', ascending=False)
print(' '.join(high_earners['Name'].tolist()))

hints.level_1_nudge: Filter df using df['Salary'] >= 50000 and sort using .sort_values(by='Salary', ascending=False).
hints.level_2_strategy: Extract names with high_earners['Name'].tolist() and join with spaces.

lessons.title: apply, drop_duplicates & Missing Value Handling
lessons.concept_markdown:
- `df.apply(func, axis=0/1)`: Applies custom functions across columns or rows
- `df.drop_duplicates()`: Removes duplicate rows
- `df.fillna(value)`: Replaces missing `NaN` entries with imputation constants or metrics

code_walkthroughs.title: Transforming Values with apply
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
print(s.apply(lambda x: x * 2).tolist())
code_walkthroughs.explanation: `apply` runs the lambda on each element, doubling each value.

practice_challenges.title: Missing Value Mean Imputation
practice_challenges.description: Read a space-separated line of tokens where missing numbers are written as `'nan'`. Convert into a Pandas Series of floats. Impute any missing (`NaN`) values with the mean of the available numbers. Print the imputed values rounded to 1 decimal place, space-separated.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Impute missing values with mean
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

tokens = input().split()
vals = [np.nan if x.lower() == 'nan' else float(x) for x in tokens]
s = pd.Series(vals)
imputed = s.fillna(s.mean())
print(' '.join(f'{x:.1f}' for x in imputed))

hints.level_1_nudge: Replace 'nan' with np.nan, create Series s, and use s.fillna(s.mean()).
hints.level_2_strategy: Format numbers with f'{x:.1f}' and join with spaces.
hints.level_3_clue:
s = s.fillna(s.mean())
print(' '.join(f'{x:.1f}' for x in s))

lessons.title: Split-Apply-Combine & Group Aggregations
lessons.concept_markdown:
GroupBy follows the **Split-Apply-Combine** paradigm:
```python
df.groupby('category')['metric'].mean()
```
- `.agg({'metric1': 'sum', 'metric2': 'mean'})`: Applies multi-metric aggregations
- `len(grouped)`: Number of distinct groups
- `grouped.size()`: Row count per group

code_walkthroughs.title: Department Average Salary
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'Dept': ['IT', 'HR', 'IT'], 'Salary': [90000, 60000, 110000]})
print(df.groupby('Dept')['Salary'].mean().to_dict())
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Splits by department and computes average salary per department.

practice_challenges.title: Top Genre by Revenue
practice_challenges.description: Read an integer `N`. Then read `N` lines containing `'Genre Revenue'` (e.g. `'Action 150.5'`). Group movies by Genre, compute total revenue per genre, and print the genre with the highest revenue along with its total revenue rounded to 1 decimal place as `'Genre: Revenue'`.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
# Group by Genre and find highest revenue
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
rows = []
for _ in range(n):
    p = input().split()
    rows.append({'Genre': p[0], 'Revenue': float(p[1])})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
grp = df.groupby('Genre')['Revenue'].sum()
top_genre = grp.idxmax()
print(f'{top_genre}: {grp[top_genre]:.1f}')

hints.level_1_nudge: Use df.groupby('Genre')['Revenue'].sum() to compute group totals.
hints.level_2_strategy: Find top genre using grp.idxmax(), and print f'{top_genre}: {grp[top_genre]:.1f}'.

lessons.title: pd.concat & Relational pd.merge Joins
lessons.concept_markdown:
- `pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=0)`: Stacks DataFrames vertically (row-wise)
- `pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)`: Combines DataFrames horizontally (column-wise)
- `pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='inner'|'left'|'right'|'outer')`: SQL-style joins on primary/foreign keys

code_walkthroughs.title: Merging Users and Purchases
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
users = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'name': ['Alice', 'Bob']})
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'item': ['Book', 'Pen']})
merged = pd.merge(users, orders, on='id')
print(merged[['name', 'item']].to_dict('records'))
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Performs an inner join matching on `'id'` key across both tables.

practice_challenges.title: Inner Join Price Lookup
practice_challenges.description: Read an integer `N` for products table (`Product Price`). Read `M` for sales table (`Order Product`). Perform an inner join on `Product`. Compute total revenue (`sum of prices of all orders`) and print it as float rounded to 1 decimal place.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# Read products and sales, merge on Product, compute total revenue
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
prods = []
for _ in range(n):
    p = input().split()
    prods.append({'Product': p[0], 'Price': float(p[1])})
df_p = pd.DataFrame(prods)

m = int(input())
sales = []
for _ in range(m):
    p = input().split()
    sales.append({'Order': p[0], 'Product': p[1]})
df_s = pd.DataFrame(sales)

merged = pd.merge(df_s, df_p, on='Product', how='inner')
print(round(float(merged['Price'].sum()), 1))

test_cases.description: Product not found omitted by inner join

hints.level_1_nudge: Merge sales and products on 'Product' using how='inner'.
hints.level_2_strategy: Sum the Price column of the merged DataFrame and print round(total, 1).
hints.level_3_clue:
merged = pd.merge(df_s, df_p, on='Product', how='inner')
print(round(float(merged['Price'].sum()), 1))

sessions.title: Session 24 - Vectorized Strings, DateTime & Pivot Tables

lessons.title: Vectorized .str, .dt Accessors & Pivot Tables
lessons.concept_markdown:
- `.str`: Vectorized string methods on Series (`s.str.upper()`, `s.str.contains()`, `s.str.strip()`)
- `.dt`: Vectorized DateTime operations (`s.dt.year`, `s.dt.month_name()`, `s.dt.day_name()`)
- `df.pivot_table(index=..., columns=..., values=..., aggfunc='mean')`: Multidimensional aggregation tables

code_walkthroughs.title: Vectorized DateTime Day Name
code_walkthroughs.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-02'])
print(dates.day_name().tolist())
code_walkthroughs.explanation: Converts strings to timestamps and extracts weekday names using `.day_name()`.

practice_challenges.title: Pivot Table Regional Sales Sum
practice_challenges.description:
Read an integer `N`. Then read `N` lines formatted as `'Region Product Sales'`. Construct a pivot table summarizing total sales with `index='Region'`, `columns='Product'`, and `aggfunc='sum'`. Fill missing cells with `0`.
Print the total sum of sales in `'North'` region across all products as an integer.
practice_challenges.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# Compute total sales for North region from pivot table
practice_challenges.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
rows = []
for _ in range(n):
    p = input().split()
    rows.append({'Region': p[0], 'Product': p[1], 'Sales': float(p[2])})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
pvt = df.pivot_table(index='Region', columns='Product', values='Sales', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)
if 'North' in pvt.index:
    print(int(pvt.loc['North'].sum()))
else:
    print(0)

test_cases.stdin:
4
North Widget 100
South Widget 200
North Gadget 150
North Widget 50

hints.level_1_nudge: Use df.pivot_table(index='Region', columns='Product', values='Sales', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0).
hints.level_2_strategy: If 'North' in pvt.index, sum row pvt.loc['North'].sum() and cast to int.

questions.title: Customer Segmentation & Churn Analysis
questions.description:
Read an integer `N`. Then read `N` lines formatted as `'Plan Churned'` where `Plan` is string ('Basic' or 'Pro') and `Churned` is integer `1` (churned) or `0` (retained).
Compute the churn rate percentage for each plan: `(churned_count / total_customers) * 100`. Print the plan with the higher churn rate as `'Plan: Rate%'` rounded to 1 decimal place (e.g. `'Basic: 40.0%'`). If equal, print `'Tied'`.
questions.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# Compute churn rate per plan and print higher churn plan
questions.solution_code:
import pandas as pd

n = int(input())
rows = []
for _ in range(n):
    p = input().split()
    rows.append({'Plan': p[0], 'Churned': int(p[1])})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
grp = df.groupby('Plan')['Churned'].mean() * 100
plans = grp.index.tolist()
if len(plans) == 2 and abs(grp[plans[0]] - grp[plans[1]]) < 1e-5:
    print('Tied')
else:
    top = grp.idxmax()
    print(f'{top}: {grp[top]:.1f}%')

hints.level_1_nudge: The mean of a 0/1 column multiplied by 100 directly gives the percentage rate.
hints.level_2_strategy: df.groupby('Plan')['Churned'].mean() * 100 gives rates per plan. Compare values.
